Glasgow.region: Glasgow and the west of Scotland
Glasgow.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Glasgow and the Clyde
s1loc: Glasgow runs one of Scotland's largest visitor economies, drawing millions of trips a year. The marquee draws cluster along the Clyde and the West End, from the Zaha Hadid Riverside Museum and the Tall Ship Glenlee to Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, the country's most visited free attraction. Glasgow Cathedral, the Necropolis, the Gallery of Modern Art and the Glasgow Science Centre with its IMAX and Glasgow Tower round out the headline list.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. Pollok Country Park and the Burrell Collection, the People's Palace and glasshouse on Glasgow Green, the Botanic Gardens and the Hidden Gardens at Pollokshields draw families, while Glasgow Green watersports, the Pinkston paddlesports centre and the cycling at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome keep activity operators working. The Buchanan Galleries and Argyle Street shopping quarters and the Merchant City add steady year-round footfall.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the Mackintosh trail and the Glasgow School of Art to the Tenement House, the Trades Hall and Provand's Lordship. The OVO Hydro and SEC Armadillo anchor the Scottish Event Campus, while the Theatre Royal, the King's Theatre, the Citizens Theatre and the Celtic Connections, West End and Merchant City festivals fill the events calendar across Finnieston and the Old Town.

Underpinning it all is a deep city-centre hotel trade through the Merchant City, Finnieston and around George Square, supported by a wide tour-guide scene and the Celtic Park and Hampden Park stadium tours. Glasgow Central and Queen Street stations, the Subway, the Clydeside ferries and Glasgow Airport at Paisley bring visitors in from the doorstep, with Loch Lomond and the Trossachs a short day trip out.

Edinburgh.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Edinburgh and the Lothians
s1loc: Edinburgh carries one of the UK's busiest visitor economies, drawing millions of trips a year. The marquee draws run along the Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle, with its Crown Jewels and Stone of Destiny, down to the Palace of Holyroodhouse, taking in St Giles' Cathedral, the National Museum of Scotland, Camera Obscura and the Scott Monument. The Royal Yacht Britannia at Leith and Arthur's Seat in Holyrood Park complete the headline set.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. Princes Street Gardens, Dynamic Earth, Edinburgh Zoo and the Royal Botanic Garden draw families, while Portobello beach, the Water of Leith walkway and the climbing at Edinburgh International Climbing Arena at Ratho keep activity operators moving. The Princes Street and St James Quarter shopping districts and the Christmas market in East Princes Street Gardens add a long seasonal trade across the year.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the Old Town and New Town World Heritage Site to Gladstone's Land, the Writers' Museum and the Georgian House. The Usher Hall, the Festival Theatre and the Playhouse run year-round, while the August festivals, led by the Edinburgh Festival Fringe and the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, plus the Hogmanay celebrations, pack the events calendar across the Grassmarket and the Royal Mile.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel trade through the New Town, the Grassmarket and the Leith waterfront, supported by a wide tour-guide and ghost-walk scene around the closes and vaults. Waverley and Haymarket stations, the trams and Edinburgh Airport bring visitors in from the doorstep, with Musselburgh, the Forth bridges and the Lothians coast a short day trip out from the centre.

Liverpool.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Liverpool and Merseyside
s1loc: Liverpool runs one of the country's biggest visitor economies, built around its waterfront. The marquee draws cluster at the Royal Albert Dock, from the Beatles Story and Tate Liverpool to the Merseyside Maritime Museum and the International Slavery Museum, with the Royal Liver Building and the Three Graces at the Pier Head, the Museum of Liverpool, the Liverpool Cathedral and the Metropolitan Cathedral close by.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. Sefton Park and the Palm House, Croxteth Hall and Country Park, Crosby beach with Antony Gormley's Another Place and the New Brighton seafront draw families, while the Mersey Ferries cruises, the watersports at Crosby Lakeside and the M and S Bank Arena keep activity operators and event teams busy across the season and the Liverpool ONE shopping quarter adds steady footfall.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the World Museum and the Walker Art Gallery to Strawberry Field, Speke Hall and the Williamson Tunnels. The Cavern Club, the Royal Court, the Empire Theatre and the Philharmonic Hall run year-round, while the Magical Mystery Tour, Penny Lane and a busy festival calendar across the Baltic Triangle and the Ropewalks fill the events programme through the warmer months.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel trade through the Ropewalks, the Baltic Triangle and the waterfront, supported by a wide tour-operator and guide scene and the Anfield and Goodison Park stadium tours. Lime Street station, the Mersey Ferries from the Pier Head and Liverpool John Lennon Airport at Speke bring visitors in from the doorstep, with the Wirral and the Sefton coast a short day trip out.

Newcastle upon Tyne.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Tyneside
s1loc: Newcastle anchors a strong North East visitor economy along the Tyne. The marquee draws run across the Quayside, from the Tyne Bridge and the Gateshead Millennium Bridge to the Discovery Museum with Charles Parsons' Turbinia, the Great North Museum: Hancock, the Laing Art Gallery and St Nicholas' Cathedral, with the BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art and the Glasshouse International Centre for Music on the south bank at Gateshead.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. Leazes Park, Jesmond Dene and the Ouseburn Farm draw families, while Antony Gormley's Angel of the North just south at Birtley, the Tynemouth Longsands and the watersports off North Shields, plus the Eldon Square and Grainger Town shopping quarters, keep activity operators and event teams working. The Quayside markets and the Hoppings funfair on the Town Moor add a strong seasonal pull.

Heritage and culture run deep, from Grainger Town and Grey Street to the Castle Keep, Bessie Surtees House and Segedunum Roman Fort at Wallsend on Hadrian's Wall. The Utilita Arena, the Theatre Royal, the City Hall and the Tyne Theatre run year-round, while the Great North Run, the Newcastle Mela and the Quayside seaside festival at Tynemouth fill out a busy events calendar across the warmer months.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel trade through the city centre and the Quayside, supported by a wide tour-guide scene and the St James' Park stadium tours. Newcastle Central station, the Tyne and Wear Metro out to the coast and Newcastle Airport at Woolsington bring visitors in from the doorstep, with the Northumberland coast, North Shields and the Cullercoats and Whitley Bay seafront a short day trip out.

Sunderland.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Wearside
s1loc: Sunderland is building a coastal visitor economy along the River Wear and the North Sea. The marquee draws include the National Glass Centre on the Wear's north bank, the Sunderland Museum and Winter Gardens overlooking Mowbray Park, St Peter's Church at Monkwearmouth and the Blue Flag Roker and Seaburn beaches, with the Roker Pier and Lighthouse and the Penshaw Monument standing over the city as familiar Wearside landmarks.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. Herrington Country Park, the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust reserve at Washington and the sandy stretches at Roker and Seaburn draw families, while the watersports and surf off the seafront, the Seaburn seafront play areas and the Bridges shopping quarter keep activity operators moving. The Stadium of Light hosts matches and arena concerts, adding a strong events draw across the season.

Heritage and culture run deep, from Washington Old Hall and Penshaw Monument above Washington and Houghton le Spring to the Tommy statue and the sea-glass beach at Seaham further down the coast. The Sunderland Empire Theatre and the Fire Station auditorium run year-round, while the Sunderland Illuminations, the Seaburn air show and the Keel Square and Keel Crossing events fill the city's calendar through the warmer months.

Underpinning it all is a growing hotel trade through the city centre and the Roker and Seaburn seafront, supported by local tour and guide operators working the coast and the mining heritage trail. Sunderland station, the Tyne and Wear Metro and Newcastle Airport bring visitors in from the doorstep, with the Durham Heritage Coast, Seaham harbour and the County Durham countryside a short day trip out from the city.
